utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Gagic, before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you were about to start your cross-examination. Are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gagic. I want to take you to 1991 and slightly before you went to Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, P1050.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If you'd have a look at this exert, I want you to read page 93 of the English and 70 of the B/C/S. Now, what you're going to see, Mr. Witness, is a diary by a woman called Glisic, who was the secretary to minister of defence, Simovic, in 1991. Can I presume you know who Simovic is, or was?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The theme that I want to ask you about is the town of Apatin and you've evidence about events in, I think, February of 1992, where Apatin was subject to a terrorist attack. You following me so far?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what I want to ask you about is Apatin prior to that and an attack on Apatin which took place around the time of this reference in the diary to 12th of November, 1991. Would you just have a look at the page and quickly glimpse through it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said, Mr. Gagic, please.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let just read on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I just want you to read the whole of this particular entry with reference to the title: "When the town of Apatin was left without protection."

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the next, until we get to page 246.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then I'll ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the next page, I think, and then we're done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, obviously this describes a number of things but one of the main themes is the vulnerability of Apatin, the border town, including raids by Croatian forces and also bombardment of Apatin. Were these events that were professionally of interest to you, or, if not professionally of interest, did you learn about them through the media or through other sources?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of the serious and difficult situation in Apatin, both at the time I was there and because of the mixed population living in the area. There was also the potential risk of incursions by the Croatian army into the territory of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was this big news? Was this across the media in Serbia, the idea that Serbia was going to be drawn into the war through attacks on its territory?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The attack itself on Apatin confirmed these assumptions, and these events at Apatin were breaking news and something that was widely covered in the media; whereas, what we have read in this report here was not the subject of media interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now if we go to page 245 of the B/C/S and page 95 of the English, you can see Mr. Sokolovic, the minister of the interior of Serbia, talking about a regulated issuances of arms to the populations of Sombor, Odzaci and Apatin, but also complaining that such people like General Pekic, were involved in illegal arming. Do you know anything about Sokolovic's complaints in that regard?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically about these conversations and complaints, no. But I was aware of the fact that a certain amount of weapons were distributed outside of the legal institutions to the local population who abused or misused the weapons they received, either by reselling them or by opening fire when it wasn't strictly necessary to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware of discussions within the Ministry of Interior concerning how to deal with the protection of Apatin and the border towns, with one option being the formation of an anti-terrorist unit?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of these discussions or the idea to form an anti-terrorist unit in the area. I don't think it could have gone further than entertaining this idea because there was an anti-terrorist unit in Novi Sad, which is not very far from this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know, then, why Badza called upon members of the RSK MUP to assist when Apatin was invaded by terrorists in February/March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apatin had not been taken by a group of terrorists in March of 1992. Rather, there was a terrorist group on the move in the area between Sombor and Apatin. Now, the reason why Radovan Stojicic, Badza, called in representatives of the Krajina MUP and volunteers was that he refused to receive a unit of ours, lest we weaken the protection of the border areas, since there were partial combat activities still going on in Slavonia. Now, the police in Serbia had already been preoccupied with problems in Kosovo, so between 20 to 30 per cent of effective police forces from Serbia were dispatched to Kosovo to maintain law and order there. The third reason, in my view, was the fact that in order to neutralise this terrorist group, they needed a group of individuals who had combat experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the -- you've told us last week that the SAJ under Badza, did engage in combat in Eastern Slavonia but was that, as far as you were aware, the first time that they'd engaged in proper combat?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Admittedly, this was before my coming to Slavonia. The anti-terrorist unit did take part in combat and had sustained casualties among its ranks. So they did engage in proper combat and not just in providing protection and security of persons and facilities which is what they went on to do at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So just to understand the timing, they'd engaged in proper combat in late 1991 and some of their number had been injured during that combat, in that period of time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-1991, they became involved in combat, so I got there in -- in late 1991, and by that time, they had already been deployed to the Slavonia battle-field, and in the months of July and August, before September of 1991, they had taken part in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were injured in the same year? Or some of their number, I should say.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them were wounded in 1991. As far as I know, during the later stay of that unit in the Slavonia battle-field, no one came to be wounded. That's to say, after the month of September of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just before you move from this document, let's go to the page 246, the last page of this exert, and I want to ask you if you know anything about General Simovic's comment there, when he notes that the Ministry of Defence, or: "We have been asked by the government of the Serbian Autonomous Region of Krajina to set up a training camp in Prigravica, records need to be made." Were you aware that the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina were looking to the Serbian Ministry of Defence to assist them with training their combatants and the place where they sought to form a training base was in Prigravica? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of that. Prigravica is in the territory of Serbia; in other words, not in Slavonia or in the Republic of Croatia. It is close to Apatin and to the brotherhood and unity bridge I testified about earlier on. I think that this initiative from the SAO Slavonia, Baranja, Western Srem, or the SAO Krajina coincided with the setting up of a training ground's centre in Erdut. By that time the idea had ripened and requests were sent, and the top police and military leadership decided - I don't know exactly when - that the training centre should be set up in Erdut, rather than Prigravica, which lacked the necessary infrastructure for such training grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tendered this as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objection. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Actually, it is already part of an exhibit. I beg your pardon, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, at least certain portions are in evidence, including the ones you referred to. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I have some more of the same book to show the witness, but I think I will wait until the break to save some time. And I ask that the witness look at the pages over the break. Can we go, please, to 1D5008. And it's a judgement from the district court in Sombor. And what I'm interested in is the first eight pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I want you to just go through that very quickly just to confirm that this is the judgement which arose from the terrorist attempted incursion into Apatin in February/March 1992. If you recognise the facts, then please say so?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise the facts? If we go to the next page, just so you're clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then if the Prosecution don't object, I would just like to tender these first eight page, which summarises the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be some problems in just admitting, or just tendering, the first eight pages if it is uploaded as one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll upload it, the first eight pages, with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will have to do that then separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise these facts as reflecting the incident you've spoken about, which led to Operation Amfibija?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then I'll apply to tender the first eight pages in -- perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And once they are uploaded, we will reserve a number for them. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserve number for first eight pages of 1D5008 will be D695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Now, just moving you backwards a little bit to when you went to Eastern Slavonia, you spoke last week about the tasks that you were performing. Am I correct that your tasks were wholly limited to crime prevention or crime detection activities? You and your unit, I mean.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. The unit focussed on prevention. And my engagement outside of the unit was of a mixed nature, both prevention and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Training of who? And for what?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the training side of the story is my engagement in the formation of the the Secretariat of Internal Affairs in Vukovar, based in Dalj, inasmuch as I was making certain suggestions and giving advice about admission of staff into that secretariat, the way to organise it, and adjusting legislation to the newly arisen situation because the territory of Slavonia and Baranja did not have an institutionalised legal system or a legal framework, whereas, the laws of the Republic of Croatia had ceased to apply with the establishment of Krajina, so it was necessary to start applying the laws that were in force in Serbia. So I had an instruction role in teaching them how to apply the legal regulations from Serbia, and, in the beginning, how to draft Official Notes and reports about incidents and, later on, we also worked on regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's a lot of description. But are we talking about police work when you're talking about regulations, when you're talking about Official Notes and reports about incidents, and so on? Are we talking about police work? Crime prevention work?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was part of the police work. Police regulations, criminal regulations, criminal and trial rules; whereas, the prevention aspect in combatting crime was my presence in other police stations that were then controlled by the authorities of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that is to say, western Baranja and Srem, and instructing staff, because very few of them were trained policemen. Most of the former trained policemen had left, and police stations at that time were staffed by less than 50 per cent of the professional policemen. New admissions were regular citizens who wanted to work in the police and met certain criteria so they were employed, they were hired, without actual police training.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think what you said was that you went -- arrived there on the 29th of September of 1991. At this point, most of the combats had finished; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The combat had just started then. The combat and the final operations in Vukovar only started in end November that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. The police work that did you, was this the same for all your colleagues who went with your unit, and also the unit that went to Knin, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the unit that went to Knin, I don't know any details. All I know is that that unit did not stay in the same composition as when it left because many of members of that unit joined the police and army units in that area that were more developed than in Slovenia. So the unit did not remain integral. In fact, I think they ceased to exist a month after they were set up. As far as the involvement of my unit is concerned, only I was actually involved doing this training and instruction; whereas, the rest of the unit, all of them, only manned check-points on the bridge, apart from the first ten days when we were busy organising our own accommodation and doing some patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did -- did -- let me just move you forward very briefly to 1995. Did you hear about Serbian MUP police officers, about 400, being sent from Serbia and Kosovo to Banja Luka to conduct similar crime prevention activities?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about MUP units sent outside the territory of Serbia. The same happened in the territory of Slavonia, only a bit later, after the liberation of Vukovar, after the -- the end of fighting in Vukovar. Some more units were sent from the MUP of Serbia to re-establish law and order, and I think two units were sent to the area of Slavonia towards Sid and Tovarnik. Not the upper part, closer to Erdut and Dalj. And I know about the sending of units to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And that was under the authority of Badza. Am I right about this: About 400 men were sent to try and restore some sort of law and order in the towns some distance from the front lines? Does that accord with what you know?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The units were sent on Badza's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, I just want to make it clear to the Court. You haven't spoken to the Stanisic Defence team before coming to court, have you? We haven't contacted you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's return to 1991. You testified about checking traffic across the brotherhood and unity bridge. Again, you were checking for illegal possession of arms in the main; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to clarify that a bit. A two-prong check was done on that bridge. One check was done by my unit, which, in terms of establishment, belonged to military police; but in addition to us, there was a unit of military police made up of professional troops who checked military vehicles; whereas, my unit checked civilian vehicles, in order to avoid bottle-necks and jams on the bridge. In addition to preventing the traffic of arms and spirits across the bridge, because alcohol was banned, we also looked for some items that were in shortage to prevent smuggling, and we were trying to prevent the export of property from Slavonia and Baranja as a form of combat against looting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Just let me return - sorry - briefly to the issue of the 400 police officers in Banja Luka. You said that the units were sent on Badza's orders, and I just want to clarify who told you that and how you came by that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present when the unit was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Where was that; and when was that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was present in Belgrade when the unit was departing from a police training ground called the Zvezdara woods in Belgrade, and I knew many people from the unit. Some of them from before; some from the days of war; and I had just come to say good-bye.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And who else was present from the Serbian MUP? Was --

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On behalf of the Serbian MUP, Obrad Stevanovic was seeing the unit off. And there were other higher- and lower-ranking officials of the MUP. Certainly around 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And was that meeting a briefing of sorts, where the objectives and purposes of the mission were laid out clearly for you to hear?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that meeting was not a briefing. There were too many people for a briefing. Somebody made a short farewell speech, wishing them to return alive and in good health and to be successful in the tasks they were given. It was just a short speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And why were you present?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said. There were no less than 20 of my friends from the service within the units that were departing. I had come privately without an invitation, without being part of the organisation, just to see them off. It's a kind of tradition where I come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And before I move on, I just want to understand as clearly as possible where your understanding came -- where your understanding came from in relation to what their tasks were going to be. Was it from that meeting or prior to that meeting or -- or where did you learn that their job was to be normal police crime prevention jobs?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I learnt earlier that the unit would be departing, and I had even expressed my desire to go with them. However, my bosses did not allow me to go because the incidents of violent crimes in Belgrade was high, and this was complex work, and my superiors thought that I would be more useful dealing with this job in Belgrade than if I left with the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have -- let's move to a different subject. 1D02568, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to deal with the subject of General Boro Ivanovic, who you mentioned you had seen him coming to Erdut on several occasions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's, Your Honours, page 17141.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, could I just stop you from reading for a moment? Were you aware that Ivanovic was tried in a military court for a number of disciplinary offences, amongst them illegally giving arms to the RSK; and, secondly, collaborating and co-operating and giving weapons to Arkan and the Tigers?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there were some trials, but much later, after 1995. However, at the moment when I met General Ivanovic, I did not know that he was tried by a civilian or military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the document very quickly. It's a 1st Army intelligence document sent to the chief of the General Staff of the VJ, 22nd of September, 1994, and contains a number of allegations against Ivanovic, along the lines as I described.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 of the document, and 2 of B/C/S, please, sorry. Three of the English and 2 of the B/C/S. You'll see a record or a note there about collaboration between the military organ and the MUP, establishing Ivanovic's registration of certain cars, and his association with, as quoted there, "persons prone to criminal activity, particularly Zeljko Raznjatovic." And you'll see there at the paragraph beginning with, "during 1993 ...," an allegation that Ivanovic is effectively using military registration plates to provide Arkan with the means of crossing border crossings. Is something that you learnt about at the time or learnt about it afterwards, Arkan using registration plates provided to him by Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that then, and I actually see this document for the first time. I don't know how true it is because the relationship between Arkan and the people from the MUP was much closer. So Arkan did not need registration plates from Ivanovic, unless they were military registration plates. And there is no reason why a general of the army would be providing licence numbers to Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But you can confirm - am I correct - that Ivanovic was collaborating with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say that Arkan was collaborating with Ivanovic because Ivanovic was the more important personality, at least at the time when I was there. There was co-operation between the two. It was visible. I, myself, saw them together at least five times. I know that they even planned some activities in that area together. And I know that they co-operated closely later and were involved in some criminal dealings, like the cutting of a forest, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So Ivanovic and Arkan were involved in smuggling? Is that what you're trying to convey to the Court? And, in particular, the smuggling of the wood from a forest that they cut down?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it that way. I don't know if "smuggling" is the right word, but they cut the wood illegally and sold it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we find out what the source of knowledge of the witness is in this respect. How did you learn this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came back, I left behind many people with whom I remained in touch, and from talking to those people who had remained in Slavonia, I learned that the wood was being cut and sold without any official institution standing behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know if we've covered this, but I want to be clear. Ivanovic subordinated Arkan to -- to him to conduct various combat operations in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did that continue into 1992?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do have a statement from Ivanovic -- not a statement that we took. It's a potential exhibit. But if the Prosecution don't dispute this subordination, as the witness has just testified, then I don't need to put the statement to him because in the statement Ivanovic admits to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under what Rule would you put it in, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would ask the witness about the facts in this statement and I would ask it to be admitted as an exhibit pursuant to 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the statement was taken for the purposes of the ICTY proceedings, you said? Or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, it was taken in relation to these military disciplinary proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's first ask Ms. Friedman. Is there any dispute about resubordination?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I don't think we have enough details about the subordination on the basis of this witness's knowledge. I can't say at this time that we don't dispute it. As for the statement, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you one thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. You say: I don't think we have enough details for the subordination on the basis of this witness's knowledge. Now, what I understand is that Mr. Jordash wants to ask you whether there was any dispute about a matter even for the purpose of not bothering this witness with it. So your answer that, On the basis of the statement of the witness, we're unable to say whether it is in dispute, that seems to be a bit a circle reasoning.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I take your point, Your Honour. The issue of Arkan's subordination to the military is definitely a key issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. And is it in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... more documents, if I may. Coudl I, fist of all, ask for this to be tendered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We do have any information on the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can it can be MFI'd until we provide the information, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, this document to be MFI'd will receive the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2568 will be Exhibit D696, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please, 1D02510, please. Sorry, 1D2570.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what should be coming up, Mr. Witness, that you, I hope, will be able to help us with is more information, a report on bringing Major Ivanovic before the military disciplinary court, dated the 6th of August -- sorry, the 6th of October, 1994. And just for your information, because we won't have time to read through everything, but this is a fairly comprehensive report, or purports to be, at least, on the various disciplinary offences alleged against Major-General Ivanovic. And it -- and it deals with his removal from duty while he is being investigated. And if we go to page 4. No, let's stay -- sorry. Let's go back to page 2. And we see there an allegation at number 1, alleging that as the Chief of Staff and commander of the Novi Sad Corps in the period from the 6th of January, 1992, to 2nd of August, 1994, he: "Abused his official position and exceeded the bounds of his official authority by acting in contravention to orders of the president of the FRY and the General Staff of the VJ Chief of Staff and the orders of the commander of the 1st Army forbidding the issuance of equipment and materiel for use and utilisation outside of the units and institutions of the Army of Yugoslavia," and so on? And if we go over the page, we'll see the volume which is alleged 2.337 -- no I think that's 2 ... 2.337.179 pieces of various kinds of ammunition and weapons and at least 205.725 litres of fuel. Were you aware of these allegations against Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware that he gave Arkan two tanks in 1991?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see the tanks, but I didn't know how the Arkan's Tigers had come by them. I didn't know if it was the result of war assets having been redistributed or some sort of gift, though the latter was highly implausible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you aware, as is alleged in this document, that it was recommended that Ivanovic should be pensioned off, lose his job, as a result of his conduct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The facts related here clearly indicate that General Ivanovic could clearly have been not just pensioned off but even have had his employment terminated because these amounted to serious practices of abuse of official position. Probably in view of his many years of service in the army, it was concluded that he should be pensioned off and then prosecuted as a retired officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, could we try to clearly found out what the witness knows and what kind of conclusions he draws from documents, Probably this is the case, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you commenting on the seriousness of the allegations as laid out in the document; or are you commenting on facts you know from outside of this document concerning Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I have never seen this document before, I could not have based my testimony on this document; rather, on certain facts that I know from before. And my comment is that this amount of 2 million-odd pieces of weapons is exaggerated. As far as fuel is concerned, I think that it had to do with excessive consumption, which was admittedly still within bounds, and probably the army had entrusted the amount of fuel to third parties in the field without going back and checking up on what they were doing, without putting in records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, do you have any knowledge whether Ivanovic was ever prosecuted for these facts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that criminal proceedings were instituted against General Ivanovic post-1995. He had not been prosecuted earlier on or during the period I was in contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what, then, did these criminal proceedings result in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of the outcome of the proceeding. I don't think, though, that General Ivanovic was convicted. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was he acquitted? I mean, did he have to appear before a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not aware of the details concerning his trial because he was tried before a military court, and they do not allow to have a public gallery that would follow the proceedings before that court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it a military disciplinary court, or was it a military court which would impose sanctions as if it were a normal criminal case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, it was a military court, not a military disciplinary court. Rather, a military criminal court, which would have imposed the same sentences civil courts would impose in keeping with the legislation in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you think he was not convicted. Was he then -- what -- what happened if he was not convicted when he had appeared before a court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know the facts. I can only guess. As I've said, these court proceedings were conducted behind closed doors, and I was never taking much interest in that. I had never been a friend of General Ivanovic's to have any personal interest in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it is as well possible that he was acquitted or at least that he was not found guilty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not rule out the possibility that he may have been found guilty but imposed a rather lenient sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just don't know; is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I tendered this as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We would await information on provenance for the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: MFI, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2570 will receive number D697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Mr. Jordash, it comes as a bit of a surprise that you couldn't even tell us where such a document which you apparently used with the witness comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just could I just have a moment, please? Can we have a few moments? We will be able to find out, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have 1D02235, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, in order to avoid that everything remains unclear on the transcript, I asked, or, I said that I was a bit surprised that you had no knowledge about the provenance and then you said you asked whether you could have a few moments so as to be able to find out. I do not know whether it was perhaps overlapping speakers which might cause some problems at a later stage to finally make the transcript. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I have just a minute to consult, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Stanisic received the documents from -- directly from Zoran Lilic, who obtained them, in some way, from the military security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We would -- we have tendered official documentation when we have received documents from official authorities, so we would prefer to that that -- I can -- yeah, we would like to have more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you verify whether -- you said you have documents as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, Your Honour. The Prosecution -- our practice is when we tender documents to provide the official correspondence and we do think that it's important to maintain that level ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, there isn't any official correspondence because they were handed directly from Lilic to Mr. Stanisic. That's the route by which they came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, might be slightly different to be in the OTP or to be an accused to receive some documents from another person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. But it is somewhat problematic for us to accept the word of the accused about provenance. This could lead to problems down the road. I can -- we will have to consider our position on this further, but for now we would like it to remain MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It remains MFI'd for the time being. Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly. And I think the Prosecution could check with Mr. Lilic too. He's one of theirs, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me -- I don't want to take you through this whole statement, Mr. Gagic, because it is quite detailed and contains Ivanovic's response to the allegations. But I do want to take you to page 12 of the English and 7 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any date for the document, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. I -- perhaps we can go to the last page which contains the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says at least it was quarter past 5.00 in the afternoon. That is the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll try and find a date. We can probably time it with other documents, though, but we'll try and find a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let go back, then, to page 12 of the English and 7 of the B/C/S. And we'll find out what Mr. Ivanovic purports to say about his relationship with Arkan: "Asked to explain his acquaintance and relations to Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic, aka Arkan, he replied, 'I met Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, in the Slavonia theatre in 1991, but I don't remember exactly when or where. In the course of combat operations, he was assigned to me several times to carry out combat assignments with his men. He carried out combat assignments and nothing else. I am not beholden to him in any way, nor is he to me, and we do talk on the phone or call on each other. And if we run into each other, we exchange greetings because we have fought together in the war, and I am making no bones about that. I have no other relationship with him. When I was Chief of Staff, he used to come and to see General Biorcevic at the command post on board the Kozara vessel, where we also used to meet.'" From what you've told us, is this correct? From what you've told us, Ivanovic is not quite being as candid about his relationships with Arkan as he would have wanted the disciplinary proceedings to believe. Do you accept that? Do you see my point? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Obviously, according to this, General Ivanovic would like to make his war contacts with Arkan public, whilst denying any other contacts that they may have had outside of performing combat assignments. He is obviously trying to suppress any other contacts he may have had with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the date seems to be the 2nd of August, 1994, if I look at page 2, but ... of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Sorry, I missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We have a few issues with this document. There is, of course, the provenance issue, but also anything, any statement of a third party admitted under 89(C) should be subject to scrutiny. We have always presented arguments as to why a particular statement is reliable and why it is admissible. In this case, this is a self-interested statement of somebody being investigated. Also the witness did not appear to have much knowledge about anything in the document. So we would have to consider it further, but we do think that the Defence would have to meet the threshold of 89(C).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Provenance, Mr. Jordash, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was the Lilic issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Lilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And we agree with the Prosecution. It's not a reliable statement. It's a statement which we accept Ivanovic did not tell the truth. What it does do is say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, if I understood the position of the Prosecution well is reliability, is whether it is or is not that it's unable to assess the reliability, and not that the Prosecution agrees with you, that doubts as to the reliability of the statement brings you together.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I thought we agreed about something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, did I understand your position well?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't understand then the position. If the Prosecution suggests that the statement isn't reliable or the contents of the -- that it isn't a genuine statement from Ivanovic. Is that the position or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that not having the details that the Prosecution would need a further, perhaps, verification of -- of whether or not this document can be considered to be an authentic, whether the content of this statement reflects the truth, yes or not, and that you are unable to do so at this moment. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And it depends very much on the circumstances of each case, but in this -- for the reliability of a statement we need to consider the way it is taken and other corroboration. Whether it can be -- whether it is the most appropriate way to put the evidence on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I suggest that we give some time to the Prosecution to look at that and have it MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. I would also add to that the Prosecution could shortcut all of this by deciding what is a very narrow point, whether they accept Ivanovic was -- did subordinate Arkan to him on several occasions and did have a -- a relationship which also went beyond -- this is a very -- an issue that the Prosecution ought to have a position on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman -- I think that Ms. Friedman explained that this is not a matter on which she can agree at this moment, just as simple as that. And I'm getting more and more confused because you said it wasn't a reliable document; wherein -- whereas in this document, Mr. Ivanovic says that he assigned combat tasks to Arkan which ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it is our position that Arkan was in the main subordinated to Ivanovic and Biorcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's reliable in that respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you told me that you agree with Ms. Friedman that it's not a reliable statement. But now I do understand that you consider it, at least in this respect, reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In that respect, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm just trying to understand your positions which are perhaps a bit more complex than reliable or not reliable. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2235 will receive number D698, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we take a break Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We are late already, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In that break, may I give -- I will have the witness look at a section of Exhibit P1050, to save time after the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please be so kind to read during the break the document that will be given to you. We will take a break, and we will resume at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I just want to return to the subject of Ivanovic allegedly providing military registration plates, because I think that there might have been some misunderstanding on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honours, line -- sorry. Page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I showed you the document which is now D696 MFI, and I asked you the question: "And you'll see there at the paragraph beginning with the, 'during 1993 ...,' an allegation that Ivanovic is effectively using military registration plates to provide Arkan with the means of crossing border crossings. "Is that something that you learnt about at the time or learnt about it afterwards, Arkan using registration plates ..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise to the interprets but it is very important. My colleague, Mr. Jordash, put the question very precisely, identifying the kind of plates that were provided, and in the B/C/S interpretation this was not specified. I apologise to everyone, but this is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you read the question again. I do not know exactly what the reason is, why you expect there to be a confusion, but let's just -- if you slowly read it again, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I -- perhaps I could summarise it what I think is the confusion and ask the witness to deal with it in a more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I heard the answer of the witness earlier, I wondered whether he had any factual knowledge, that is, as a matter of fact, because he started explaining the why and the why not. That's at least what I remember. I would have to re-read that. And we should carefully find out what the witness knows about it or whether he finds it logical or illogical or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The -- what I'd like to do is ask him about -- if there was a confusion in his mind and then I'd like to take him to the document again and ask him some questions about the source of the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we start by just reading again to him the question and the answer and then ask him whether this is the answer he intended to give, and then we'll find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I want to try to understand whether we've understood each other. The question I asked you was based on: "... an allegation that Ivanovic is effectively using military registration explanation plates to provide Arkan with the means of crossing border crossing. "Is that something that you learnt about at the time or learnt about it afterwards, Arkan using registration plates provided to him by Ivanovic?" And you answered: "I didn't know about that then, and I actually see this document for the first time. I don't know how true it is because the relationship between Arkan and the people from the MUP was much closer. So Arkan did not need registration plates from Ivanovic unless they were military registration plates, and there is no reason why a general of the army would be providing licence numbers to Arkan." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you first ask the witness whether -- what was read to him reflects his answer. That seems to be the first relevant question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you follow that, Mr. Witness? Was that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether what was read whether that reflects the answer you gave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the next question, the first one, at least, would be: What personal knowledge do you have about military registration plates provided by Ivanovic to Arkan? Do you know anything about that, whether that happened or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that Arkan used vehicles with military registration plates, he drove a car with civilian licence plates, or without any licence plates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do we then have to understand your answer that, not knowing about what happened as far as licence plates are concerned, that you told us whether you considered it to be logical or illogical, that he would have been provided by Ivanovic with military registration plates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems illogical to me that Arkan would have used military licence plates. It seems -- it makes more sense to me that would have used civilian ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. That's what I -- that's how I understood your answer, that you wanted to explain to us how logical, or, as a matter of fact, how illogical it was that it would have happened as stated in that allegation. Is that what you intended to bring to our attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, whatever further questions you have -- I had some concerns about factual knowledge and -- or, conclusions on logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you shouldn't understand this as to be exhaustive. If you have anything else on your mind, please don't hesitate to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The document where this allegation was made was a document authored by somebody called Commander Colonel-General Jevrem Cokic. Did you, or do you know that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that general.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you mentioned Kostic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it would be fair for me to help my colleague, Mr. Jordash. First of all, we don't have the right page. The name is on a different page. And it was pronounced as Cokic, although it's Jeverem Sokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- now, I take it that perhaps the interpreters have made Mr. Kokic Mr. Cokic, because I take it that that is how it is supposed to be pronounced. There was some question about whether you have been provided with the right name. I think you were. But does the name of Colonel-General Jevrem Cokic say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Kosutic means something to you, though; is that right? Kosutic.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosutic was not a general at the time, as far as I know. I know he was a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting he was. But was he part of the military security or intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was an officer of the military security.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And would he have known about Ivanovic's collaboration with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was aware of that co-operation because he was present there - at least when I was - in the Slavonia theatre of war. Colonel Kosutic was there at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And despite being aware of that collaboration, are you able to -- do you know anything about whether he reported that to his senior officers or to the unit that he was part of?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether he reported it or not, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: He certainly didn't express or indicated to you or anyone else that he regarded that as a problem, did he, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, because I'm speaking about the early days, 1991, 1992, when the relations were more of a military and professional nature. These events dealt with in the documents you've shown me relate to 1993, 1994, 1995, so what Kosutic later reported, I don't know. But, at the time, when I was there, he did not ask for any consultation with me, nor am I aware that he had sent any report about irregularities in the conduct of Arkan or General Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to what you know about military code at the time, would you have expected him to report that; and, if so, do you know why he didn't?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, in the period when I was there, there were no such irregularities, at least they were not pronounced. They began later. As to whether Kosutic sent reports about it later, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, I just want to deal with one more subject. The trial of the Skorpions, or members of the Skorpions for the murders at Trnovo, what was your involvement with that prosecution?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in those criminal proceedings in my role as chief of service for the detection of war crimes in the MUP of Serbia from 2004 until 2006, and one of the cases that crossed my desk were the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It crossed your desk in what sense? Can you be concrete as to what you did in relation to that prosecution.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a longer story. I will try to put it briefly. At the request of the War Crimes Prosecutor, I came to his office and I was told that a videotape would be viewed. I put certain conditions before the playing of that tape because there were some people present there who were not from the police or from the office of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm running out of time and I want to be as specific as can I be. Did you have a part to play in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My job, after receiving that videotape, was to arrest the men identified from the videotape and bring them before an investigative judge, and that's what I did, with my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you there present during the investigation, or at least part of the investigation by the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Apart from the interview conducted on the premises of the police, which was my right and my duty, I was not involved in the pre-indictment proceedings, I did not attend the interrogation by the prosecutor, or by the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So you -- you interviewed the various suspects as part of your police duties; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I did not conduct all the interviews myself because there were many suspects, and the time for their bringing into custody was short so that my various team members conducted some of the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you remember the interviews that you did conduct, the names of the suspects?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should like to look at the document that I have in my bag here, if possible. But, if not, I spoke to the two Medic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why would you want to look at the document in your bag? What is it and how would it help you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document lists all the men arrested in that operation, and I would not like to make a mistake about some names or some other details concerning them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you think you interviewed more than the two Medic brothers? Or was -- or were you only involved in those two interviews?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke only to the two of them, and very briefly. My operative workers spoke to them in greater detail. My job was to co-ordinate the whole activity so I couldn't put aside five or six hours to speak to one person alone. My job was to co-ordinate, to work out the schedule for bringing them before the judge, so I didn't speak to any of them in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were you part of a team, then, who gathered the results of the interviews, i.e., that you shared the information that had been gathered from the interviews to work out what to do next in the investigation?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not conduct detailed interviews. We relied on the story told us by the perpetrators, because the case was developed by the prosecution who had already collected some evidence already. And we were only asked to bring those persons into custody. The prosecutor had all the documentation for the investigating judge ready. So we just conducted a short interview to confirm their identity and to link them to the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: All right. And am I correct from your interviews with the Medic brothers and the information you gathered during that investigation, none of the suspects were alleging that the Skorpions were under the command of the Serbian DB. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I think the witness has already indicated that he wouldn't be in a position to answer. And I think Mr. Jordash is trying to get around that. Having not asked about the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not having asked doesn't exclude for the possibility that someone spontaneous makes an observation. That's a ... The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Am I correct? None of the suspects, according to the evidence you received during the interviews of the two Medic brothers or information you gathered as part of the investigation, were alleging that the Skorpions were under the command of the Serbian DB at the time of the offence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the suspects alleged they were members of the State Security Service of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In fact, I'll take it one step further. None of them were saying that they were even under the Serbian MUP, were they?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I knew those facts already.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the period from receiving the documentation based on which we were to start the operation for their arrest, until that moment, ten days had elapsed, and I used that time to study the Skorpion unit. And, in that time, I already established they had no connection with any establishment in Serbia, either the Ministry of Interior or the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May we have on the screen 1D01321.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you engaged with this investigation until the final judgement of the trial of the Skorpions?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you engaged with this investigation until the final judgement delivered by the War Crimes Court? The judgement, as you can see on the screen, which was delivered on the 10th of April, 2007.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was involved. But apart from the initial activities to arrest them, I was engaged only once later in arresting one person that I believe was not part of the first batch of arrests, and collecting some additional information about that person, there were no more requests for me. So my involvement ended when I arrested them and brought them before the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we go to page 55, please, of the English and 58 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to ask you about various parts of the judgement and see if it accords with the information you gathered during the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the witness has told us that he was not involved in the -- apart from studying that. So let's be careful there. And let's first ask him whether he knows anything about A, B, or C, and then, if he know, then we can compare that with the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems to be the appropriate way of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me see if you can agree or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness starts reading already parts of ... Could you please stop reading and first focus on Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was -- is this the information that you gathered during the investigation; that, firstly, that the Skorpions were paid by the company NIK? They were employees of that company.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were on the payroll of that company.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And from what the suspects were saying at that time, no one else paid them. It was -- their income came from the Krajina Oil Company; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And their income was quite sufficient, even higher than the income of most people who worked in that area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the suspects -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could -- could I'm just trying to find out -- could you tell us about -- you say they were on the payroll. At what point in time did you investigate that? And how did you investigate that? If you did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I knew that they were established as a service for providing security to the oil company of Krajina. I knew that because I had occasion to see them even when I was working in the Krajina. And then, later, after they were arrested and I spoke to them, they claimed they were paid until enter 2005 only as security men working for that oil company of Krajina. And later on, they received some part of their income through the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that part of the interview you had with the two brothers, that they told you this? Was that part of what was asked? And was that what they stated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They were asked, and I insisted on that question about all the sources of their income. And they told me, Our salaries at the time were quite sufficient, even much higher than the average so we didn't need any additional income. And they received their equipment from the government of the RSK; that is, the -- the fund -- the government fund of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was an Official Note made of that interview with the two brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A joint report was made. And there were no Official Notes resulting from the two separate interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this was part of the interview before -- after their arrest but before they were brought before the investigating judge. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. And may I then take it that you heard that from the two brothers but that your colleagues may have heard it from the other accused but not you, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard it myself, as did other colleagues. Because they were asking almost identical questions. So this wasn't in dispute in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But you heard it from those persons you had interviewed; and you did not directly hear it from others, which you did not interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you hear from the Medic brothers that they'd been -- who sent them to Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what did they say?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they had been sent by the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and that Milanovic, aka Mrgud, the then-minister of the defence of the RSK, or deputy minister, because his positions changed, assigned them to that task.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just take instructions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I ask you this, I don't know if you will be able to deal with this or not but are you able to -- do you know anything about the Trnovo front at the time the Skorpions were sent to the Trnovo front? Do you know anything about the military operations that had been ongoing there for some time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that there was fierce fighting at the Trnovo, which is close to Sarajevo. There was a threat from the Muslim armed forces who wanted to seize the area of Trnovo and, thus, get behind the Serbian forces. Other members of the Army of Republika Srpska had to be engaged elsewhere, in other fronts, and care had to be taken to ensure that the area did not fall into Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And before I ask you how you know this, do you confirm this: That if Trnovo had fallen, Sarajevo and Pale would have been encircled? Are you able to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is a bit too wide an area to say that Sarajevo and Pale would have been encircled. Pale would have been encircled, indeed; whereas to encircle Sarajevo, it would have taken much more than that line coming from Trnovo, but Pale would definitely come under threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So basically Trnovo was critical for the survival of Pale and the headquarters of the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That position was highly significant and had to be defended by stronger forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And how do you know that? What's your source of knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to know all these facts only at the time I started working on the Skorpions case. Before then, I had heard of Pale but not of Trnovo and the threat against Trnovo. I got to know all these details whilst I was working on the case involving the Skorpions and the arrests that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you about one aspect of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash. Mr. Jordash, could you -- next time could, you please first ask about the knowledge. Because -- the source of knowledge. Because, to some extent, you've asked opinion from the witness rather than knowledge. I mean, his assessment of what would happen, et cetera, et cetera. So I think if we stick to facts and then we know the source of knowledge of those facts, and then it is clearer, separated from opinion, because there was quite a lot of opinion that you asked the witness -- or at least he gave opinion in his answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: How did you get these details about the importance of Trnovo to Pale?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a briefing with a prosecutor, the one I was just about to tell you about, and, on that occasion, I learned all the details related to the case, to that particular event. The prosecutor briefed me on the broader context and background to these events because, by then, the prosecutor had prepared much more voluminous material than had actually been forwarded on as part of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And am I correct that the prosecutor never briefed you, suggesting that there was a link between the military operations in Trnovo and the military operations in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of these facts before I viewed the tape. And once I viewed the tape, the prosecutor told me that regardless of the fact that Trnovo was 150 kilometres away from Srebrenica, the individuals had most likely come from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Ms. Friedman, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? You would say, apart from the furniture, you are?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you return it to Mr. Jordash, he has tasked you with something.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps can I deal with that by -- through the bar table procedure with the Prosecution later. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And discuss it with Ms. Friedman. I have got no idea what the document is about, so I can't express any -- any opinion on that. Mr. Gagic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Friedman. Ms. Friedman is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gagic. Can you hear me clearly?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You testified that in September 1991, two units of volunteers from the Belgrade SUP joined the military units in the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Two units were set up. They didn't join; rather, they became military police units. As they were leaving Belgrade, they were already military police units, as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And most of these police officers had originally come from Croatia. But just to be clear, at the time that these military police units were comprised, all -- all of you were employed by the Serbian MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the Belgrade SUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Which fell within the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Belgrade SUP was one of the units within the organisation of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you continued to be employed by the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia even as the military police unit within the Novi Sad Corps [sic]; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you reported at that time to the head of the Territorial Defence, Radovan Stojicic, also known as Badza; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My unit's commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Badza -- was Badza your unit's commander then?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Badza was the commander of the overall TO Staff; whereas, our unit had its commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And that was Veljko Bogunovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And Veljko Bogunovic reported to Badza; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You testified that when you arrived: "A number of SAJ, special anti-terrorist units, headed by Radovan Stojicic, Badza, were also there in Slavonia." That's at T.17122. And these officers were also employed by the Serbian MUP at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Was this unit, the SAJ unit, also referred to as Plavi at the time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The unit didn't have a name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the presence of a unit called Plavi?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Though there were a great many units with various names, so I cannot rule out the possibility that there was one such unit, although I can't say that I had known about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, back to the SAJ unit. You said it doesn't have a name. How is it referred to? How did you know who I meant? What name should we attribute to it to make it clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
