utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that my learned friend is trying to confuse the witness. The Prosecutor did quote what the witness had to say about it in -- in direct examination. But he was talking about elements of that unit in Slavonia, not about the unit as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please refrain from analysing and -- the testimony tells us what the witness said. You may make an objection if you want to, but preferably not in this way. Let me have a look at the --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could I rephrase my question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you would first give me an opportunity to re-read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may rephrase it. But I may have a comment after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I asked you just a moment ago about the SAJ anti-terrorist unit that was present already in Eastern Slavonia when you arrived, and after, when I asked you if they were called Plavi, you said they didn't have a name. So I just wanted to clarify were they called then the SAJ anti-terrorist unit? Is that their name?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the SAJ. They were only a part of it. There were ten to 12 at the most, and they never worked as a unit. They worked as individuals who were there next to the TO Staff commander, Badza. They never functioned as a group and had a name as a group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My comment would be that you ask the witness about the unit he spoke about earlier. And then to later ask him, How did you know which I meant, you had clearly indicated that you meant to refer to the unit the witness testified about it. So, therefore, that was a question which should have left out.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is now very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: According to your testimony, these members of the SAJ unit trained Arkan's Men, and also: "Participated in the execution of combat actions, and they also worked on the security of the TO headquarters and personally security of Radovan Stojicic, Badza." Are you aware whether they also were engaged in escorting prisoners from Baranja to Eastern Slavonia, travelling through Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you described the people who were billeted in Erdut as the -- along with you in -- about ten days later, as the commander of the TO unit with his deputy and assistant and members of the special anti-terrorist unit who were securing the commander and his deputy and also performing other tasks. So does that refer to Badza, Zavisic and the SAJ members?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It refers to Badza.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And was his deputy Zavisic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the rest of your question. I'm sorry. Yes, it does refer to Commander Badza, Trajkovic, and Zavisic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did any other units or members of units of the Serbian MUP police arrive -- of the Serbian MUP arrive after you, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that two units arrived, but that was only after the combat activities in Vukovar ended. So it could have been December of 1991 or January of 1992. Of these two units, two police stations were set up, but these two police units and stations gravitated towards Sid, which was a different area of Slavonia. I wasn't in -- in contact with them frequently, but I did have occasion to see them there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So when you arrived in September, between your units and the ones already there, there were probably about 50 to 60 Serbian MUP police officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly 60. With my unit and the rest who were there, including, Badza, Trajkovic, Zavisic and all the others, well, just under 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know who Badza was reporting to?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I can draw my conclusions. He reported to the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia and the commander of the corps under which he was engaged in combat. And so he would be reporting to these two structures, but when and under which circumstances, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you were asked in direct examination who you placed yourselves under. But your unit, I presume, did not decide who would be its commander. This was decided by the Serbian MUP leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, when you testified the other day, you said that the permission -- or, first, just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we also try to find out exactly what the basis of the knowledge of the previous answer is. You confirmed that your commander -- who your commander would be was decided by the Serbian MUP leadership. Do you know any further details about -- did he tell you or -- how did you become aware of who had appointed your commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I joined the unit literally one day before the unit set off. I was away for private reasons and was not working for some ten or so days. So that, by the time that I heard that the unit was being set up, I went to the location where the unit was supposed to gather, and by that time there was already the leadership structure in place. Later on, in conversation with Rade Markovic, who was the chief the SUP in Belgrade, I was told that it was the minister himself who suggested that Bogunovic be appointed the unit's commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In the summary of your evidence provide by the Simatovic Defence team, it originally stated that the deployment was approved by Rade Markovic. And then we received a correction that you made shortly before the testimony where you said that the minister was actually Sokolovic, not Markovic. Now when you testified the other day, you said that the permission for the unit was granted by: "The then-chief of the Secretariat of Interior, Rade Markovic, and the then-minister of the interior, at the time, Radmilo Bogdanovic." You then corrected yourself, saying that Zoran Sokolovic was already minister by then. And my question to you is: Whether that slip of the tongue is actually due to the fact that Bogdanovic did still continue to play a big role from behind the scenes although Sokolovic was minister.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The slip came about because the ministers changed in a very short period of time so that, hence, the slip of the tongue, Radmilo Bogdanovic was the minister for a couple of months; whereas, Zoran Sokolovic was there for a few months only. So most of these events and goings-on were related to Bogdanovic. But I am not aware of the fact that Radmilo Bogdanovic continued playing a prominent role after Sokolovic replaced him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When you say "most of these events and goings-on were related to Bogdanovic," which events and goings-on are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the specific situation at hand. The war that was in the offing, the events in Lika, the log revolution. All the various events that characterised 1991, or roughly the summer of 1991. And for most of that period, the minister was Radmilo Bogdanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We heard evidence that there was a meeting in September 1991 at the Belgrade SUP where the situation in Croatia and the need to send police there was discussed. It actually took place in the theatre, in the Belgrade SUP building. I take it you were at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such meetings happening on a daily basis. There wasn't just one. I attended some of these meetings whenever my acquaintances from the war-affected areas had requests made of me to forward them at these meetings. Also to my crime police service, I also had access to the chief of the Belgrade SUP where I would convey the information. So the meetings were held periodically but the conclusion was that there was nothing we could do but exert additional pressure on the JNA to protect the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you attend a meeting, though, discussing your deployment to Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I joined the unit. There was no meeting. I joined the unit, and then I informed my superiors of the fact that I had joined a unit only at the time when it was quite clear that I would be a member of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, these other meetings that you said were happening at the time that you did attend, was Mr. Stanisic ever present?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You testified that you continued to be employed by the Serbian MUP. Isn't it also a fact that the Ministry of Defence would not have a record of you being a member of the army, nor someone who had been engaged in professional military service as an officer, non-commissioned officer, or professional soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The leadership of the army must have information that I was a member because I had received a military police ID with my photo on it indicating my P.O. Box, to which I belonged, in the Novi Sad Corps. Such a document must have been recorded in the archives of the army, and that applies not only to me, but all 40 members of my unit. We all had such IDs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, just to be upfront with you, I'm not going to call up this document right now, but we've asked for such a record from the Ministry of Defence and they've returned a letter stating that they don't have any record of you being a professional soldier or registered with a Territorial Defence organ. So, that's their position on it. Does -- would you dispute that? And ...

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I can prove it. I mean, I can't prove it, but I believe there are members of my unit that still have that ID, and I believe I could get it, get such IDs through my lawyer, and he would submit them to you later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. We have seen, as well, your military ID. What I'm talking about is a bit different. We'll see. Perhaps I will show you that document. We can resolve it. But moving on for now. You stated that you did not take your Serbian MUP ID with you and you took your military booklet instead. Was this a specific instruction that you received from the Serbian MUP leadership?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you crossed into Croatia carrying personal side-arms; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So crossing into Croatia without MUP ID and not being a JNA soldier, armed, would have been illegal at the time, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in principle, it would be illegal. But since this was an organised crossing, in a bus bearing police markings, we crossed quite normally. Nobody asked any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And you stated that: "The forming of the unit and its departure to Slavonia was no secret, nor was there any reason for the formation of such a unit to be secret." Now, it was no secret to you, but surely if you did not have your Serbian MUP IDs, then the fact that you were Serbian MUP employees must have been a secret to some people in the area.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not for a moment was the fact that we were members of the MUP hidden from the locals or others. On the contrary, we insisted on it. We emphasised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Was it also not hidden, then, to the UN forces when they arrived?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was concealed from the UN because very soon after their arrival, I left the area at my own request, and I didn't have any contact with the UN. But whether anyone concealed our presence from them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you testified that in addition to your personal arms, you received additional weapons from the TO defence arms depot; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you stated that these types of weapons, based on what they were, they could have been weapons belonging to the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA or the Territorial Defence. Those were infantry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: But my understanding is that you don't have any specific knowledge as to how the weapons arrived in that TO depot, how or -- or when.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And your information that Arkan's Men got their supplies there, from my understanding, was based on seeing one of their vans at the depot on one occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the ammunition being loaded onto the vehicle, not by the depot. The vehicle could pass by the depot on any account whatsoever, even when the combat equipment is being loaded.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just to -- I just would like to confirm that that's the only information you have on how Arkan was armed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even just by looking, I noticed that members of his unit had weapons that was, until then, the exclusive prerogative of the JNA. The paramilitaries did not have access to that kind of weapons. But when I saw those weapons in their hands, I knew that they were being supplied by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I think this would be -- I believe it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: It would be a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, before the break, I asked you about your records, or lack of records with the Ministry of Defence, and you stated that you had an ID that you could ask your lawyer to produce. Could you explain, please, what kind of ID you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been a misunderstanding. There is a separate ID unrelated to the military booklet that I gave to you and that is still in the secretariat. It's an official ID of the military police of the Yugoslav People's Army. I didn't mean to get it from my lawyer. I meant that through your lawyers I would, perhaps, get that document to you from one of the members of my unit, because my own ID has been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I see. So this is a Territorial Defence -- a military police ID; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when was yours destroyed?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My copy was destroyed during the bombing of the MUP building in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the other -- you said that some other members of your unit may have theirs. Those are members of your military police unit in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean those 40 members of the unit who went with me. I think - in fact, I'm sure - some of them still have their IDs.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you give us any of their names so that we could check, follow up on that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Bogunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: He was the commander?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ninko Tarbuk, Dusan Knezovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And your military ID was maintained at the building of the MUP Serbia? It was kept there?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That military police ID was in my locker in the building of the MUP of Serbia, but it was in my desk. I didn't have time to get it out because a few days before the bombing of the building I was on field mission, so I failed to pick up my personal things, and many of my personal items, including that ID, remained in the desk and were destroyed during the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move on to a different area.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can we please have D303, MFI.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gagic, you have already been asked about this report during ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the formal status, of course, is --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- still confidential so that it should not be shown to the public or the status should change and just say, We all agreed, there was actually no reason for it. That is, in itself, not sufficient. Therefore, would you apply to change the status or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would apply to change the status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then other parties. Do I understand -- provided by Mr. Stanisic. Any objection, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber relies on the accuracy of what the parties have told the Chamber. D303 becomes a public document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, you saw this document last week, and it's a report of the Serbian DB dated the 3rd of May, 1991. And it states, quote -- it states - sorry - that the situation has: "Led some representatives of the Serbs in these areas to turn to the Serbian MUP for help in the form of a greater presence of JNA units in the wider area." Do you recall looking at this document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document here, at this trial, a few days ago. I had no occasion to see it before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you testified that you assumed that the political pressure was exerted: "... for the MUP to have the army get out of the barracks and to carry out patrols and secure the area in this matter." Is it your evidence that the intention was for the army to perform policing work rather than aggressive attacks?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's how we can interpret it because the police forces in that area did not exist, apart from the police force of the MUP of Croatia. They did not deal with keeping law and order. They were causing unrest rather than suppressing them and it was necessary to have a presence of some uniformed organs to restore peace and to prevent disturbances.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the document is marked strictly confidential, and if we look at the top right of the document, we see that there's also a caution that says: "Return after reading!" This comment, "Return after reading!," indicates a very high level of secrecy. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And it is uncommon, isn't it, to see this type of instruction on an information report or an Official Note like this one.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may sound unusual to you but it is not at all unusual. I don't see from the document to whom it was sent. I can only see who authored it, but I don't see to whom it was sent. But it's normal even when sending something to the highest leadership like members of Parliament to ask them to return the documents after reading rather than keeping them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So you say that you've seen this type of remark before?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen documents that I was required to return after reading too. But I didn't see this document and this type of document that I was not a recipient of except here, at the trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, you were asked last week to view a video-clip containing remarks of Branko Kostic, vice-president of the SFRY Presidency. And you said that: "People are given promises that they would be protected from an escalation of conflicts and that they would be provided safety to alleviate the fears that they felt toward the Croatia police." Is it your evidence that your deployment in September 1991 was connected to the fear that the Serbs in Eastern Slavonia felt as a result of Croatian police officers?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When you arrived in Dalj, though, in September 1991, it had already been taken over by the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: After the JNA had entered on the 2nd of August; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the only police forces in Dalj at that time were comprised of police officers of Serbian ethnicity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also policemen of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were the people -- was the police force predominantly Serb though?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat what you just said. You said: "Yes. But ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police force was very small numerically, insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And it was the same in Erdut and all of SBWS, in fact, wasn't it, that there was no longer a predominantly Croat police force. It was at that time predominantly ethnic Serb?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of Eastern Slavonia and Baranja had a police force of precisely that composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I see, actually, that one of your answers is not recorded in the transcript. I asked after whether when you arrived it was after the JNA had already entered. And you answered "The Territorial Defence." And then I asked "After the JNA entered on the 2nd of August; isn't that right?" Could you repeat your answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer was yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That was just to fill in the transcript. Now, you testified last week that as a result of your work, you would communicate with large numbers of policemen from other republics and therefore knew a lot of policemen who came to Serbia after they'd left Croatian service on their own or were dismissed. So, you testified that: "The majority of them contacted me asking me to help them resolve their status." Did you inform the Serbian DB about who had contacted you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Would the Court Officer please display 65 ter 1D2439. The document is entitled: "List of suspended (fired) police employees in the territory of Slavonia and Baranja, engaged in the defence of certain locations."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I want to ask you -- I take it you recognise some of the names on this list?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, there's a pen at your desk. I would like -- on the screen in front of you, I would like to ask if you can take that pen.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the Court Usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you put a check mark, please, next to the people that you know.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You know, I realise, actually, that it may be a little hard to tell, just because of the pen, not you. Could you maybe just read into the record the numbers of the people that you recognise, not their names.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. [Interpretation] Number 1; number 2; number 6; number 8; number 12; 16; 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And before we move to the second page, I just want to ask whether any of -- first of all, to the best of your knowledge, is this information true that they're originally from Croatia and were dismissed from their positions but then serving elsewhere still in -- in Slavonia and Baranja?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning those I knew personally, I knew they were members of the service. I knew they were all deployed, and I met them all there. In fact, I -- I didn't know them before that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were any of them people that had requested employment first in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These are men who had never relocated from Slavonia. I was approached by people who hailed from other parts of Croatia who were unable to stay in their native territory, and these are men whom I met when I went to Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And now can we have the second page, please. And -- I think, in B/C/S -- yes. Good. That's right. The third in English; second in B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And can you name in the first section? Are there any more people?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of the names, up to 24, I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And under Osijek?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And Beli Manastir?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know any of these people to be operatives of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know any of them to be sources who provided information to the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that they were associates or sources of the service. The service would keep that in strict secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the second man on the list, Dragan Lazic, was this the man that you were advising and instructing on setting up police stations?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, he was appointed minister or deputy minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I worked with him, gave him certain instructions, and I had quite a lot of contact with him. He also had a brother whose name I forget. They are twins, and they look pretty much the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did he also become, at the time that you were in Eastern Slavonia, the head of the Vukovar SUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time he was appointed to a very high post. I believe he was even deputy or assistant minister, in fact, of the interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And since it was a separate entity, he was practically minister of the interior of that part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So, I presume, though, you're talking about a later period, though, when the Republic of Serbian Krajina was established? I had first intended to ask you about September 1991 and what role he had then. I understand that to be a -- or, rather, October, the -- just limited to the police. But was he already a minister in the government at that time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he became a cabinet minister during my tenure there. He was assistant minister officially but he was functionally minister for that part of the territory because the Knin part of the territory was separated from the rest, and he was practically minister for -- for that area. And I met him only in mid-October, not immediately upon my arrival. He was working as the leader of the SUP of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And at what point, then, did he hold that position until as leader of the SUP of Vukovar? From mid-October until when?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't tell you with any certainty, and I wouldn't like to guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And this document that we have before us created by the Serbian DB in Belgrade, were you aware that they were keeping track of the police officers who were engaged in Slavonia and Baranja?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you agree that when the document says that these individuals are "engaged in the defence of certain locations" this suggests a common interest shared by the Serbian DB who authored the document and the Serbs in the area as mentioned in the document?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say whether the DB had a vested interest or not. All I know is that most men from this list were employees of the public security section before they left the service or were expelled from the service.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: The public security section of the Croatian MUP; is that right? Or do you mean something else?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I'm finished with this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, it was provided by the Stanisic Defence. We don't have any information on provenance. We'd like it to be marked for identification until such time as it is received.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm hesitating because it seems slightly topsy-turvy to use a document suggesting that it's reliable, and then to query its reliability at the end of using it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman, it is uncommon to say that we first want to know whether it's -- where it comes from. That's usually the language used if you oppose the admission of a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: As we have expressed earlier and I can give a fuller position, but we do not want to tender private collection documents without having information on provenance. For now, the witness is here, and I thought he could provide some information on the document. So it would be worth getting that information at this time. But we would not want to tender it before we can have a better idea of its authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time, of course, you went to the content of it. But let's consider what that situation is. But before we do that -- Witness, at the top of the document you see, you see under the date "ZH." Do you know what that stands for? You see it in the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it. Those are the initials of the person who drafted the document. Based on that, you can identify which employee wrote this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And do you, by any chance, know anyone with the initials ZH working in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the State Security Service, and I really don't know. I can't think of anyone with the initials ZH, and I've never seen the initials on any other document before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The number of the document would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2439 will receive number P3080, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about whether you ever heard of Mr. Simatovic being at a dinner or ceremony after the fall of Vukovar, and you responded that you had not. But you were not actually looking for information, trying to gather information about Mr. Simatovic at any point, were you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Mr. Simatovic did not attend a single dinner that I attended. I have also said I haven't heard of him attending any other meeting that I didn't attend. But it's true that I wasn't gathering any information on Mr. Simatovic, and I didn't have the right to.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you were never -- you've not been employed at the Serbian DB or successor, BIA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And to this day, you may not know that some of the people that you were working with were from the Serbian DB; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't rule out the possibility. But I can't confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know that -- that Ilija Kojic worked for the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you must specify. What do you mean by "worked for"? Was an employee? Was an agent? Or was a source?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Our case and our evidence is that he was an employee. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you have other information, though, that suggests that he was an agent or a source?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have information that he was a registered agent, but in view of the fact that there was a war on -- so I don't have information that he was a registered agent. But in view of the fact that there was a war on, he may have -- it could not be excluded the possibility that he may have furnished the state security in the Republic of Serbia with certain information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you first said, "I have information that he was a registered agent," or that how it's recorded. But is your answer that you don't know he was a registered agent but he may have given information to the state security. Is that how I understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is this: I don't know that he was an active employee of the state security or that he was a registered agent of the State Security Service. And I assume that he did provide the State Security Service with information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Why do you assume that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because that was a sort of principle. Certain events of security interest for the Republic of Serbia, the information about those events -- those events, would also come from the war-affected areas.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And Radoslav Kostic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Had you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear of him. Actually, at one point, when Radoslav Kostic was killed, I thought that another Radoslav Kostic, aka Labrador, was killed. And it was only then that I realised that they were two different people. Before then, I wasn't aware of the fact that there were two different Kostics.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear that Radoslav Kostic, even in 1991, was an employee of the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge whatsoever of his employment, including whether he was working for the public security station. What I did hear was that he was a policeman in one of the local police stations. That was the information I had at the time he was killed. At first, I was surprised to hear that he was a policeman in view of his involvement in military activities. But then I learned that they were two different people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And lastly, we heard evidence in this trial that Dragan Lazic, this man that you were assisting in setting up the police stations, worked in the Serbian DB. So my question to you is whether he ever told you that.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 6228.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Dusan Momcilovic: The Glina public security station consists of the active complement, the reserve complement and the civilian sector working on administrative affairs. The active complement consists of former employees of this public security station and new employees who have proved that they are professionals in combat operations. Since there is still a state of war in the Glina municipality, we need such personnel for future operations and, if necessary, to guard the border. The reserve complement also consists of the former reserve force and volunteers who have proved themselves in combat together with the former reservists and found their place and role in this public security station. "As regards the reserve and active complements, right now, we are short of materiel. Not everyone has the same ... standard uniforms, adequate weapons, or motor pool. As regards uniforms, we are getting help from Serbia for the time being. Blue police uniforms and blue winter uniforms from the reserve ... "Reporter: ... tell us about the co-operation between the public security station and the Ministry of Interior of the Serbian Krajina. "Dusan Momcilovic: The Glina public security station is part of the Knin Ministry of Interior, and we have receive all our tasks and requests from Knin. We respond directly to the -- we answer directly to the Ministry of Interior in Knin. We also co-operate very well with the Municipal Assembly as the organ of authority that finances us, together with the MUP ... at the same time, we carry out crime scene examinations and other applications and requests that need to be processed through the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia. Various kinds of forensic analysis and other material aid, while professional literature and the Law on Internal Affairs organs, that's at the level of the Krajina ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In this interview, Mr. Momcilovic stated that the Glina public security station carried out forensic analyses and other applications and requests through the Serbian MUP. It's quite clear that the police stations in Eastern Slavonia received personnel from the Serbian MUP. Aside from that, can you -- are you aware of any other instances where they made additional requests and received additional assistance?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hope that I understand the gist of your question, though it didn't come clear in interpretation. In order to have a fully functioning police apparatus, there needs to be an integrated system. At the point in time where this system broke through in the Republic of Croatia, links were re-established with the MUP of Serbia. For this reason, various forensic analyses such as drug analysis, et cetera, were being done in the Republic of Serbia because they could not be done in Croatia, whereas the RSK did not have forensic offices of its own. I did say earlier on in one of my answers that we did have these blue winter uniforms, which means that some of them were provided to this particular police station as well. Aside from that, what else could there have been? Well, perhaps a vehicle would be set aside for the purposes of a police station. As for the rest, I don't see what else the MUP of Serbia could have done without going through the RSK MUP.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, I just want to quote to you a part of an interview that, unfortunately, did not appear in this clip, but we will add it and it can be verified. And in this end part, Momcilovic says that: "Since we are in a state of war, the Glina public security station is ready to join the struggle against the enemy at any moment and offer any kind of help necessary to all the organs of the Glina municipality." So my question to you is whether this willingness to join in on the struggle and offer any assistance also reflects the attitude of the police stations in Eastern Slavonia in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police force of Eastern Slavonia, as well as the police force in Knin, was ready and prepared to provide assistance to all the organs who needed it. Now, what their abilities were is a different matter, but whatever they had at their disposal they were prepared to place -- to -- to -- to use, to help other organs that needed it in Krajina and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And I just have two more questions today. From the time that you arrived Eastern Slavonia until the time that you left, had the Serb-held territory expanded?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Actually, that's my final question then for the day. Thank you, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I expect to use the first session. I think no more, but possibly, I would say, up to hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would try to conclude in the first session. Mr. Gagic, we'll adjourn for the day. We'll resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 14th of February, at a quarter past 2.00 in the same Courtroom II. And I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak nor communicate in any other way, with whomever, about testimony, either given, or still to be given. We stand adjourned.
